=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

## Headline view

The Seller's package is not "fair and balanced." Taken together, four provisions would strip out most of the Buyer's protection:

- general disclosure of the whole data room and public registers;
- a constructive buyer-knowledge bar;
- one set of limitations applied to "all Claims of any nature"; and
- fundamental, tax and IP claims folded into the general cap and time limit.

The Seller's own Disclosure Letter also contradicts its Update. The Update says Bluefen is "addressed," Riverlark will be dealt with "following Completion," and the incident is "not expected to be material." The Letter says no Bluefen consent exists, Riverlark is unpaid with security undischarged, and the incident investigation is unresolved. We should rely on the Letter's facts, not the Update's characterisations.

**The "FINAL / not to be re-opened" framing.** The preamble's claims about market practice and "principal-level settlement" are Seller advocacy. Before treating any position as agreed, confirm with Wattlebridge's principals what, if anything, was actually agreed. Nothing in a counterparty's cover note binds us. Even if headline numbers (cap, basket) were agreed in principle, the mechanics around them (carve-outs, disclosure standard, knowledge) plainly were not.

---

## A. Transaction-structure issues (price and completion)

### 1. Riverlark facility (~AUD 3.2m): release "following Completion" is unacceptable
- This is inconsistent with the debt-free/cash-free baseline. The DD-003 change-of-control clause (8.1) is likely triggered by the sale itself, so the Company could be in default the moment we complete.
- Undischarged security would sit over the target's assets, and possibly its shares, after we have paid.
- **Push for:** repayment at Completion out of the price via the funds flow, against a lender payoff letter. At Completion we should receive a deed of release, PPSR financing change statements (or an undertaking to lodge within a short fixed period), and the return of title documents. The payoff amount (principal, interest, break costs, fees) should be treated as Indebtedness and deducted from the price. Back this with a specific indemnity for any residual Riverlark liability.

### 2. DD-005 completion bonuses (AUD 420k) are missing from the funds flow
- These are change-of-control transaction costs incurred because of the sale, which makes them a classic debt-like item. "A matter for the Seller" means nothing unless the funds flow reflects it. Otherwise the Company, and so the Buyer, pays.
- On-costs are not addressed. Indicatively:
  - NSW payroll tax at 5.45% ≈ AUD 23k;
  - possible superannuation at 12% ≈ AUD 50k, depending on whether the bonuses are ordinary time earnings;
  - workers' compensation premium impact;
  - PAYG withholding mechanics.
- The continued-employment conditions may fall due *after* Completion, when the Company is ours.
- **Push for:** bonuses plus all on-costs treated as Transaction Costs or Indebtedness and deducted from the price. Amounts falling due post-Completion should be held in escrow or retention, with any forfeited amounts going to the Company and not back to the Seller. Paid through payroll with withholding. Specific indemnity for the employer liability.

### 3. Bluefen consent (customer = ~30% of FY26 revenue)
- "Reasonable endeavours" and "treated as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" is far too soft. A conditional or qualified consent would count, and the clause 11.3 conditions might never be met. The Letter confirms there is currently no consent and no evidence the conditions are satisfied.
- **Push for:**
  - a condition precedent requiring unconditional written consent from Bluefen (or consent on conditions acceptable to the Buyer in its absolute discretion);
  - evidence that the 11.3 conditions are satisfied;
  - the CP to be for the Buyer's benefit, waivable only by the Buyer;
  - an "all reasonable endeavours" obligation on the Seller;
  - Buyer participation in communications with Bluefen;
  - a long-stop date with a Buyer termination right.
- Given the concentration, also consider price protection: an earn-out or escrow tied to Bluefen retention and revenue for 12 months, or a specific warranty that no notice of termination or non-renewal has been received.

### 4. Sandbar supplier renewals (3 × AUD 110k = AUD 330k)
- The Letter itself says the three renewals must be "read together for timing/scope." Three identical related renewals look like one AUD 330k commitment split into pieces. That may have been done to stay under a material-contract or conduct-of-business threshold, and it would also defeat the de minimis if claims are not aggregated.
- The Seller has given no information on whether they are terminable, prepaid or accrued, or genuinely ordinary course. "Related" also raises a possible related-party question.
- **Push for:**
  - full copies of the renewals;
  - confirmation of when they were signed relative to any interim-period covenant;
  - unpaid or accrued amounts treated as Indebtedness;
  - a warranty that they were entered on arm's-length terms and are terminable without penalty;
  - otherwise, termination before Completion at the Seller's cost, or a price reduction.
- Related claims must aggregate for the de minimis and basket (see B3).

---

## B. Liability regime

### 1. Cap at 20% of price (AUD 4.8m)
- 20% for general warranties is arguable if we accept it as a commercial point. However, the cap must not apply to:
  - **title, capacity and authority (fundamental):** 100% of price;
  - **tax:** 100% of price;
  - **specific indemnities** (Riverlark, bonuses, Ironquay, DD-006 incident): outside the general cap, at 100% of price or uncapped for defined items;
  - **fraud, dishonesty or wilful concealment:** uncapped;
  - **covenants, leakage and price adjustments:** outside the cap.
- **Credit risk.** Harbourglass is a venture vehicle and may distribute proceeds after the sale, so a cap is worth little without someone to recover from. We should require one of the following: an escrow or retention (e.g. 10–15% for 18 months), a parent or fund guarantee, or W&I insurance. If we go the W&I route, the Seller's cap can drop, but known issues (Bluefen, Riverlark, DD-006, Ironquay) will be excluded from the policy and must stay with the Seller through specific indemnities.

### 2. Thresholds (de minimis AUD 25k; basket AUD 250k, recovery of excess only)
- A 1% basket is within range, but a *deductible* basket gives away the first AUD 250k of every valid claim.
- **Push for:** a tipping basket (once exceeded, recovery from the first dollar). Related or similar claims should aggregate for the de minimis. A lower de minimis (e.g. AUD 10k) is a fallback trade. Thresholds should not apply to fundamental, tax, indemnity or fraud claims.

### 3. Time limits: "applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise"
- This default rule is the trap. Any category we forget to carve out drops to 18 months.
- **Push for:**
  - general warranties: 18–24 months, so we see at least one full audit cycle post-Completion;
  - tax: at least the ATO amendment period plus a buffer. Typically 5–7 years, extended where an assessment is open.
  - title and capacity: the full statutory limitation period, which in NSW is 12 years for a deed and 6 years for simple contract. Sign as a deed.
  - specific indemnities: matched to each exposure, e.g. the incident and IP indemnities for 3+ years, or until the regulatory or limitation position closes.
  - fraud: no limit.
- Reverse the default so that limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims unless expressly extended.

### 4. Fundamental warranties "for administrative simplicity"
Reject this outright. If title fails, we have paid AUD 24m for nothing, so capping recovery at AUD 4.8m and 18 months makes no sense. "Simplicity" is not a reason. Title and capacity should be capped at 100% of price, use the statutory limitation period, and sit outside thresholds and disclosure.

### 5. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)
As drafted, the limitations would reach indemnities, covenant breaches, price adjustments and arguably fraud.

**Push for:**
- express carve-outs for fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment by the Seller or its representatives, from all limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions;
- the limitations to apply to general Warranty Claims only;
- non-reliance not to cut down reliance on the Warranties and the Disclosure Letter itself.

Note on the ACL: Australian Consumer Law s 18 misleading or deceptive conduct liability cannot be contracted out of. Courts may still give weight to non-reliance clauses on causation, so the fraud and warranty-reliance carve-outs should be explicit.

### 6. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"
- **Tax:** we need a stand-alone tax indemnity for pre-Completion tax, covering income tax, payroll tax (relevant to the bonuses), GST, and PAYG/super shortfalls. It should be dollar-for-dollar, outside the basket and cap, with long survival and conduct-of-claims provisions.
- **IP:** for a SaaS analytics business, IP ownership is the core of the value. Treat the key IP warranties (ownership, no infringement, open-source compliance, and employee and contractor assignments) as quasi-fundamental: a higher cap (e.g. 50–100%) and longer survival. This connects directly to the Ironquay issue below.

---

## C. Disclosure and knowledge

### 1. General disclosure of the data room and public registers (Letter 1.1–1.2)
- Disclosing "every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to" in the whole data room turns the warranties into a "check the data room yourself" exercise. "Referred to" extends even to documents we never received. "Publicly searchable corporate records" is unlimited.
- **Push for:**
  - only specific disclosures in the Letter qualify the Warranties;
  - each disclosure must be fair and specific, with enough detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature, scope and amount of the matter;
  - data room documents are disclosed only where specifically referenced against a warranty;
  - public-record disclosure limited to searches of named registers (ASIC, PPSR, IP Australia) conducted on a stated date;
  - no disclosure against fundamental warranties, tax or the specific indemnities.
- Paragraph 1.4 ("nothing admits breach… or that any consent… is required") is acceptable only if the SPA states that this does not undermine the Seller's obligations to obtain consents or discharge liabilities.

### 2. Buyer knowledge bar (cl 8.3)
- This is the single most damaging clause. It covers advisers' knowledge and *constructive* knowledge ("discoverable from the data room or public records"). Combined with general disclosure, almost every claim becomes arguable. It is not market for a buyer in a deal this size.
- **Push for:** deletion, replaced by an express statement that Buyer knowledge, actual or constructive, does not reduce any claim. Australian law on the buyer-knowledge point is unsettled, so we need this stated expressly.
- **Fallback:** limit it to the actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals, as a result of specific disclosure in the Letter. It should never apply to fundamental, tax, indemnity or fraud claims, and should never cover advisers.

---

## D. Specific risk items

### 1. Ironquay IP (DD-004 cl 7.3; DD-010 AUD 180k open)
- The Seller frames this as a AUD 180k payment issue. The real risk is ownership. Under cl 7.3, title to the SOW3 Project Materials does not transfer until *every* SOW3 fee is cleared. If fees are unpaid, Ironquay may still own code embedded in the product, which could support an injunction or infringement claim and force rework.
- There is also no receipt of payment, no confirmatory assignment, and the AUD 180k figure is unverified.
- **Push for:**
  - a CP or completion deliverable of a confirmatory IP assignment from Ironquay, plus evidence of payment of all SOW3 fees, ideally a release from Ironquay;
  - any unpaid amount treated as Indebtedness;
  - an expanded specific indemnity covering all loss from the Company not owning or being free to use the SOW3 materials, including redevelopment cost, third-party claims and lost revenue;
  - the indemnity to sit outside the cap and thresholds, with 3+ years' survival.

### 2. DD-006 export and privacy incident (~1,240 records)
- "Preliminary" and "not expected to be material" is the Seller's opinion, not a finding. The Letter confirms that access, scope and the need for notification are all unresolved.
- Paperbark likely exceeds the AUD 3m small-business threshold: Bluefen's AUD 3.6m is about 30% of revenue, implying roughly AUD 12m. The Privacy Act and the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme therefore apply.
- A suspected eligible data breach must be assessed within 30 days (s 26WH). The data-room cut-off was 22 September 2026, so that window has likely passed. We need the current status urgently: has the assessment been completed, and was the OAIC or anyone affected notified?
- Exposure includes enhanced Privacy Act penalties, OAIC action, the statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy (since June 2025), customer contractual claims (check whether Bluefen's data is involved and whether Bluefen has notification or termination rights), and reputational harm.
- **Push for:**
  - a completed forensic report and NDB assessment before signing or Completion;
  - a specific indemnity outside the cap and thresholds, unaffected by disclosure or Buyer knowledge, covering regulatory, remediation, notification, third-party and customer loss;
  - a warranty that the facts disclosed are complete and accurate;
  - retention or escrow;
  - Buyer consultation rights on any notification before Completion.

### 3. Title (DD-012 share register only)
- A share register maintained by the Company is the Seller's own record, not independent verification.
- **Push for:**
  - a full title warranty: legal and beneficial ownership, free of encumbrances, and no options, convertibles, ESOP awards, SAFEs or other rights to shares;
  - Buyer-side verification: ASIC company extract and history, PPSR search against the Seller and the shares, share certificates, and a review of issue and transfer history against the constitution;
  - pre-emption and drag/tag waivers;
  - title treated as a fundamental warranty (see B4).

### 4. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009): lower risk, but confirm
- Check how each document defines "assignment" and "change of control." Some leases and contracts deem a change in shareholding to be an assignment.
- Require the lease notification to be given at the right time, as a Seller covenant or completion deliverable.
- Get a warranty that no third-party consent is required for the sale except the ones listed.

---

## E. Known-exposure tally (indicative)

| Item | Amount | Seller's proposed treatment | Buyer position |
|---|---|---|---|
| Riverlark facility | ~AUD 3.2m + break costs | Release post-Completion | Repay at Completion; deduct from price |
| DD-005 bonuses + on-costs | AUD 420k + ~AUD 23–75k | Not in funds flow | Deduct as Transaction Costs; escrow any post-Completion portion |
| Sandbar renewals | AUD 330k | Ordinary course | Diligence; accrued amounts as Indebtedness; terminate or reduce price |
| Ironquay SOW3 | AUD 180k + IP ownership risk | Narrow indemnity | CP for assignment; broad uncapped indemnity |
| DD-006 incident | Unquantified | Not material | Specific indemnity + retention |
| Bluefen | ~30% of revenue at risk | Reasonable endeavours | Hard CP; possible earn-out or escrow |

Known items come to roughly **AUD 4.2m+ before the incident and Bluefen risk**. That is nearly the whole proposed AUD 4.8m cap, which shows why these items must sit outside the general regime.

---

## Summary of recommendations

1. **Reject the "FINAL" framing.** Confirm with our principals what was actually agreed. The mechanics have not been agreed.
2. **Riverlark:** repay and release at Completion out of the price.
3. **Bonuses:** add to the funds flow as a price deduction, including all on-costs, with escrow for any post-Completion portion.
4. **Bluefen:** an unconditional consent CP for the Buyer's benefit, an all-reasonable-endeavours obligation, and a long-stop date. Consider revenue protection.
5. **Fundamental warranties:** title and capacity capped at 100% of price, statutory limitation period, no disclosure or knowledge qualification.
6. **Tax:** a stand-alone indemnity at 100% of price with 5–7 years' survival.
7. **Specific indemnities** for Riverlark, bonuses, Ironquay (expanded to IP ownership) and DD-006, all outside the cap and thresholds and unaffected by disclosure.
8. **Fraud carve-out** from every limitation, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clause. Limitations to apply to general warranty claims only.
9. **Thresholds:** tipping basket, aggregation of related claims, thresholds limited to general warranties.
10. **Disclosure:** specific disclosure only, against a "fair and specific" standard. Delete the general data-room and public-record disclosure.
11. **Buyer knowledge:** delete cl 8.3 and add an express no-prejudice clause. Fallback is actual knowledge of named individuals only.
12. **Ironquay:** a confirmatory assignment and payment evidence as completion deliverables.
13. **DD-006:** urgent status update on the NDB assessment, a forensic report before signing, and a specific indemnity plus retention.
14. **Sandbar:** full documents and analysis. Accrued amounts as Indebtedness, or terminate or adjust price.
15. **Recoverability:** escrow or retention and/or a fund guarantee, or W&I with the known issues backed by Seller indemnities.
16. **Title verification:** ASIC, PPSR and constitution checks independent of DD-012.

**Caveats:** This review is based only on the Seller's summary and Disclosure Letter. I have not seen the SPA text or the DD-002 to DD-012 documents, so clause references and conclusions should be checked against them. Statutory points (Privacy Act/NDB timing, limitation periods, payroll tax and super treatment, ATO amendment periods) should be confirmed by NSW and tax specialists before the mark-up goes out.

If useful, I can turn this into an issues list or a mark-up instruction table for the SPA next.

- This default rule is the trap. Any category we forget to carve out drops to 18 months.
- **Push for:**
  - general warranties: 18–24 months, so we see at least one full audit cycle post-Completion;
  - tax: at least the ATO amendment period plus a buffer. Typically 5–7 years, extended where an assessment is open.
  - title and capacity: the full statutory limitation period, which in NSW is 12 years for a deed and 6 years for simple contract. Sign as a deed.
  - specific indemnities: matched to each exposure, e.g. the incident and IP indemnities for 3+ years, or until the regulatory or limitation position closes.
  - fraud: no limit.
- Reverse the default so that limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims unless expressly extended.

### 4. Fundamental warranties "for administrative simplicity"
Reject this outright. If title fails, we have paid AUD 24m for nothing, so capping recovery at AUD 4.8m and 18 months makes no sense. "Simplicity" is not a reason. Title and capacity should be capped at 100% of price, use the statutory limitation period, and sit outside thresholds and disclosure.

### 5. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)
As drafted, the limitations would reach indemnities, covenant breaches, price adjustments and arguably fraud.

**Push for:**
- express carve-outs for fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment by the Seller or its representatives, from all limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions;
- the limitations to apply to general Warranty Claims only;
- non-reliance not to cut down reliance on the Warranties and the Disclosure Letter itself.

Note on the ACL: Australian Consumer Law s 18 misleading or deceptive conduct liability cannot be contracted out of. Courts may still give weight to non-reliance clauses on causation, so the fraud and warranty-reliance carve-outs should be explicit.

### 6. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"
- **Tax:** we need a stand-alone tax indemnity for pre-Completion tax, covering income tax, payroll tax (relevant to the bonuses), GST, and PAYG/super shortfalls. It should be dollar-for-dollar, outside the basket and cap, with long survival and conduct-of-claims provisions.
- **IP:** for a SaaS analytics business, IP ownership is the core of the value. Treat the key IP warranties (ownership, no infringement, open-source compliance, and employee and contractor assignments) as quasi-fundamental: a higher cap (e.g. 50–100%) and longer survival. This connects directly to the Ironquay issue below.

## C. Disclosure and knowledge

### 1. General disclosure of the data room and public registers (Letter 1.1–1.2)
- Disclosing "every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to" in the whole data room turns the warranties into a "check the data room yourself" exercise. "Referred to" extends even to documents we never received. "Publicly searchable corporate records" is unlimited.
- **Push for:**
  - only specific disclosures in the Letter qualify the Warranties;
  - each disclosure must be fair and specific, with enough detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature, scope and amount of the matter;
  - data room documents are disclosed only where specifically referenced against a warranty;
  - public-record disclosure limited to searches of named registers (ASIC, PPSR, IP Australia) conducted on a stated date;
  - no disclosure against fundamental warranties, tax or the specific indemnities.
- Paragraph 1.4 ("nothing admits breach… or that any consent… is required") is acceptable only if the SPA states that this does not undermine the Seller's obligations to obtain consents or discharge liabilities.

### 2. Buyer knowledge bar (cl 8.3)
- This is the single most damaging clause. It covers advisers' knowledge and *constructive* knowledge ("discoverable from the data room or public records"). Combined with general disclosure, almost every claim becomes arguable. It is not market for a buyer in a deal this size.
- **Push for:** deletion, replaced by an express statement that Buyer knowledge, actual or constructive, does not reduce any claim. Australian law on the buyer-knowledge point is unsettled, so we need this stated expressly.
- **Fallback:** limit it to the actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals, as a result of specific disclosure in the Letter. It should never apply to fundamental, tax, indemnity or fraud claims, and should never cover advisers.

## D. Specific risk items

### 1. Ironquay IP (DD-004 cl 7.3; DD-010 AUD 180k open)
- The Seller frames this as a AUD 180k payment issue. The real risk is ownership. Under cl 7.3, title to the SOW3 Project Materials does not transfer until *every* SOW3 fee is cleared. If fees are unpaid, Ironquay may still own code embedded in the product, which could support an injunction or infringement claim and force rework.
- There is also no receipt of payment, no confirmatory assignment, and the AUD 180k figure is unverified.
- **Push for:**
  - a CP or completion deliverable of a confirmatory IP assignment from Ironquay, plus evidence of payment of all SOW3 fees, ideally a release from Ironquay;
  - any unpaid amount treated as Indebtedness;
  - an expanded specific indemnity covering all loss from the Company not owning or being free to use the SOW3 materials, including redevelopment cost, third-party claims and lost revenue;
  - the indemnity to sit outside the cap and thresholds, with 3+ years' survival.

### 2. DD-006 export and privacy incident (~1,240 records)
- "Preliminary" and "not expected to be material" is the Seller's opinion, not a finding. The Letter confirms that access, scope and the need for notification are all unresolved.
- Paperbark likely exceeds the AUD 3m small-business threshold: Bluefen's AUD 3.6m is about 30% of revenue, implying roughly AUD 12m. The Privacy Act and the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme therefore apply.
- A suspected eligible data breach must be assessed within 30 days (s 26WH). The data-room cut-off was 22 September 2026, so that window has likely passed. We need the current status urgently: has the assessment been completed, and was the OAIC or anyone affected notified?
- Exposure includes enhanced Privacy Act penalties, OAIC action, the statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy (since June 2025), customer contractual claims (check whether Bluefen's data is involved and whether Bluefen has notification or termination rights), and reputational harm.
- **Push for:**
  - a completed forensic report and NDB assessment before signing or Completion;
  - a specific indemnity outside the cap and thresholds, unaffected by disclosure or Buyer knowledge, covering regulatory, remediation, notification, third-party and customer loss;
  - a warranty that the facts disclosed are complete and accurate;
  - retention or escrow;
  - Buyer consultation rights on any notification before Completion.

### 3. Title (DD-012 share register only)
- A share register maintained by the Company is the Seller's own record, not independent verification.
- **Push for:**
  - a full title warranty: legal and beneficial ownership, free of encumbrances, and no options, convertibles, ESOP awards, SAFEs or other rights to shares;
  - Buyer-side verification: ASIC company extract and history, PPSR search against the Seller and the shares, share certificates, and a review of issue and transfer history against the constitution;
  - pre-emption and drag/tag waivers;
  - title treated as a fundamental warranty (see B4).

### 4. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009): lower risk, but confirm
- Check how each document defines "assignment" and "change of control." Some leases and contracts deem a change in shareholding to be an assignment.
- Require the lease notification to be given at the right time, as a Seller covenant or completion deliverable.
- Get a warranty that no third-party consent is required for the sale except the ones listed.

## Summary of recommendations

1. **Reject the "FINAL" framing.** Confirm with our principals what was actually agreed. The mechanics have not been agreed.
2. **Riverlark:** repay and release at Completion out of the price.
3. **Bonuses:** add to the funds flow as a price deduction, including all on-costs, with escrow for any post-Completion portion.
4. **Bluefen:** an unconditional consent CP for the Buyer's benefit, an all-reasonable-endeavours obligation, and a long-stop date. Consider revenue protection.
5. **Fundamental warranties:** title and capacity capped at 100% of price, statutory limitation period, no disclosure or knowledge qualification.
6. **Tax:** a stand-alone indemnity at 100% of price with 5–7 years' survival.
7. **Specific indemnities** for Riverlark, bonuses, Ironquay (expanded to IP ownership) and DD-006, all outside the cap and thresholds and unaffected by disclosure.
8. **Fraud carve-out** from every limitation, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clause. Limitations to apply to general warranty claims only.
9. **Thresholds:** tipping basket, aggregation of related claims, thresholds limited to general warranties.
10. **Disclosure:** specific disclosure only, against a "fair and specific" standard. Delete the general data-room and public-record disclosure.
11. **Buyer knowledge:** delete cl 8.3 and add an express no-prejudice clause. Fallback is actual knowledge of named individuals only.
12. **Ironquay:** a confirmatory assignment and payment evidence as completion deliverables.
13. **DD-006:** urgent status update on the NDB assessment, a forensic report before signing, and a specific indemnity plus retention.
14. **Sandbar:** full documents and analysis. Accrued amounts as Indebtedness, or terminate or adjust price.
15. **Recoverability:** escrow or retention and/or a fund guarantee, or W&I with the known issues backed by Seller indemnities.
